Baby & Child

Teething: Signs, Timeline, and Soothing Tips

Updated: July 1, 2026

This article is shown in English while its translation is prepared.

Teething gets blamed for almost everything in babyhood — and it does cause real discomfort — but it is also surrounded by myths. Knowing the typical timeline, which symptoms are genuinely teething and which are not, and how to soothe safely takes a lot of the stress out of this long, drooly chapter.

The typical teething timeline

The first tooth usually appears somewhere around six months, most often one of the bottom front teeth (the lower central incisors). The top front teeth tend to follow, then the teeth work outward and backward: lateral incisors, first molars, canines, and finally the second molars.

By around age three, most children have a full set of twenty baby teeth. But the range is wide — some babies pop a tooth at four months, others are still gummy at their first birthday, and both are usually completely normal. Timing is largely genetic. If no teeth have appeared by around eighteen months, mention it to your dentist or doctor.

Real symptoms vs myths

Genuine teething signs are fairly modest: extra drooling, an urge to chew and gnaw on everything, swollen or tender gums, fussiness, mildly flushed cheeks, and sometimes a slightly raised temperature. Symptoms usually pick up in the few days before a tooth breaks through and settle soon after.

What teething does not cause: high fever, diarrhea, vomiting, rashes over the body, or a truly ill baby. A high fever is not teething — it points to something else, usually an infection, so call your doctor rather than waiting it out. Because teething happens during the same months babies start catching more everyday bugs, it is easy to blame teeth for what is really an illness.

Safe ways to soothe sore gums

Cold and pressure are the two great teething remedies. Offer a solid rubber teether chilled in the refrigerator (not the freezer — frozen-solid teethers can bruise gums), a cool wet washcloth to chomp on, or for babies on solids, chilled soft foods like yogurt or purees.

A clean finger gently massaging the gums works remarkably well, and many babies find simple comfort in extra cuddles, distraction, and something to gnaw. Keep a bib and gentle barrier cream handy for drool-irritated chins.

If your baby seems genuinely miserable, ask your pediatrician or pharmacist about pain relief options appropriate for their age — do not guess at medicines or amounts on your own.

What to avoid

Skip numbing gels and teething tablets. Products containing benzocaine or lidocaine are not recommended for infants — they carry real risks, wash away quickly with drool, and homeopathic teething tablets have had safety recalls. The apparent shortcut is not worth it.

Amber teething necklaces are a firm no from pediatric organizations: they pose strangulation and choking hazards, and there is no credible evidence they relieve pain. The same goes for any necklace or bracelet worn by a baby. Also avoid liquid-filled teethers that can leak and anything small or breakable enough to become a choking risk.

Dental care from the very first tooth

Tooth care starts the moment the first tooth appears. Brush twice a day with a soft baby toothbrush and no more than a smear of fluoride toothpaste about the size of a grain of rice, increasing to a pea-sized amount around age three.

Dentists recommend a first dental visit by the first birthday or within six months of the first tooth. Avoid putting baby to bed with a bottle of milk or juice — pooling liquid on new teeth is the classic cause of early decay. Baby teeth matter: they hold space for adult teeth and support speech and chewing for years.

Key takeaways

  • First teeth typically appear around 6 months, with all 20 baby teeth in by about age 3 — but wide variation is normal.
  • Real teething signs: drool, chewing, sore gums, mild fussiness. High fever, diarrhea, or a truly ill baby is NOT teething — call the doctor.
  • Chilled (not frozen) teethers, cold washcloths, and gum massage are the safest soothers.
  • Avoid numbing gels, teething tablets, and amber necklaces — the risks are real and the benefits are not.
  • Brush from the first tooth with a rice-grain smear of fluoride toothpaste, and book a dental visit by age one.

Frequently asked questions

Can teething cause a fever?

Teething may cause a very slight rise in temperature, but it does not cause a true high fever. A high fever suggests illness, not teeth — contact your doctor rather than attributing it to teething.

My baby is 12 months old with no teeth — is that a problem?

Usually not; timing varies widely and runs in families. Most doctors are unconcerned until around eighteen months without any teeth, at which point it is worth an evaluation. Mention it at a routine visit for reassurance.

How long does teething last for each tooth?

Discomfort typically peaks in the few days before a tooth breaks through the gum and eases shortly after. Since twenty teeth arrive over roughly two and a half years, teething comes in waves rather than one long episode.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
